cards.title: Definition of Financial Planning
cards.content: Financial Planning is a process that involves three steps: (1) Identifying a person's life goals — what they want to achieve in life. (2) Translating those goals into Financial Goals — calculating how much money is needed. (3) Managing one's finances in a way that helps achieve those goals.

cards.title: Best Time to Start Financial Planning
cards.content: The best time to start Financial Planning is as soon as a person receives their first salary. Waiting until post-retirement, after becoming rich, or after marriage means losing valuable time for savings and investment growth.

cards.title: 1. Investment
cards.content: Deciding how much money to invest and in which instruments — where to put money so that it grows over time.

cards.title: 2. Risk Management
cards.content: Managing the risks that are always present in life. Insurance is the primary tool for risk management — it provides financial protection against unforeseen events.

cards.title: 3. Retirement Planning
cards.content: Planning finances in advance so that after retirement (when active income stops), a person has enough money saved to live comfortably for the rest of their life.

cards.title: 4. Tax Planning
cards.content: Legally arranging finances to minimize tax burden. The objective of Tax Planning is maximum tax benefit, reduced tax burden through prudent investments, and full coverage of tax breaks. Tax Evasion (illegally avoiding tax) is NOT an objective — it is a crime.

cards.title: 5. Financial Needs
cards.content: Fulfilling current financial needs alongside long-term goals. A person must balance present needs (food, housing, education) with future goals (retirement, wealth building).

cards.title: 1. Transactional Products
cards.content: Products in which regular transactions (deposits and withdrawals) take place. Example: Bank Deposits, Savings Accounts, Fixed Deposits. These are used for day-to-day financial management and savings.

cards.title: 2. Contingency Products
cards.content: Products that provide financial protection at the time of an unforeseen event or emergency. Example: Life Insurance. These products address the need for protection Against Uncertainties — not for cash management or wealth creation.

cards.title: 3. Wealth Accumulation Products
cards.content: Products designed to grow wealth — create more money in less time. Examples: Shares (Equities), High Yielding Bonds, Real Estate. These carry higher risk but offer potential for higher returns.

cards.title: Insurance is NOT a Wealth Accumulation Product
cards.content: Insurance is a Contingency Product, not a Wealth Accumulation Product. Its primary purpose is protection against risk and uncertainty — not making money. Insurance Purchase is also NOT a strategy to maximize discretionary income.

sections.title: 🔄 Risk Profile and Investment Style — Four Life Stages

cards.title: Stage 1: Aggressive Risk Profile → Accumulation Investment Style
cards.content: Young Age. A person at this stage takes high risk and aims to accumulate maximum wealth quickly. Investment style is focused on wealth accumulation — putting money into high-growth assets.

cards.title: Stage 2: Progressive Risk Profile → Consolidation Investment Style
cards.content: Age around 30s. The person becomes slightly more cautious. They want safe and secure investments. Investment style shifts to Consolidation — building a strong, stable financial base.

cards.title: Stage 3: Secured Risk Profile → Spending Investment Style
cards.content: Middle Age. The person begins spending accumulated wealth — on children's education, home purchase, family needs. Investment style is focused on Spending (using accumulated wealth for life goals).

cards.title: Stage 4: Conservative Risk Profile → Gifting and Charity Investment Style
cards.content: Near Retirement. The person takes very little risk. They accumulate money to gift to children, grandchildren, or donate to charity. Investment style is focused on Gifting and Charity.

cards.title: What is Inflation?
cards.content: Inflation is the rise in the general level of prices of goods and services in an economy over a period of time. When inflation occurs, the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services than before.

cards.title: Effects of Inflation — TRUE statements
cards.content: 1. Inflation leads to a rise in prices. 2. Inflation means erosion (reduction) of money value. 3. Inflation plays havoc (is destructive) — when inflation is very high, it damages the economy and hurts ordinary people.

cards.title: INCORRECT Statement About Inflation (Exam Trap)
cards.content: WRONG: 'Inflation means more purchasing power.' This is FALSE. Inflation REDUCES purchasing power — money buys LESS when prices rise. If inflation rises, people become more careful with spending, not less. Never select 'more purchasing power' as an effect of inflation.

cards.title: Investment Horizon and Returns
cards.content: Greater Investment Horizon (longer time period of investment) = Larger Returns. This is a direct positive relationship. Investing for longer gives more time for compounding and growth.

sections.title: ⚠️ Insurance Planning — What is Included and Excluded

cards.title: What is Part of Insurance Planning?
cards.content: Insurance Planning includes: Life Insurance, Protection of Assets (Property Insurance, Vehicle Insurance), Health Insurance. All types of insurance coverage for life, health, and assets fall under insurance planning.

cards.title: What does NOT form part of Insurance Planning?
cards.content: Housing Loans do NOT form part of Insurance Planning. A housing loan is a financial liability taken to purchase property — it is part of debt management or financial planning, but NOT insurance planning.

sections.title: 🚀 Exam Pro-Tips (Quick Memory)
items: Financial Planning = Identifying goals + Translating to financial goals + Managing finances.
Best time to start Financial Planning = As soon as one gets FIRST SALARY.
5 Elements: Investment, Risk Management, Retirement Planning, Tax Planning, Financial Needs.
Tax Evasion is NOT an objective of Tax Planning — it is illegal.
3 Financial Products: Transactional (Bank Deposits), Contingency (Life Insurance), Wealth Accumulation (Shares, Bonds, Real Estate).
Insurance = Contingency Product. Provides protection against uncertainties. NOT a wealth accumulation product.
4 Risk Profiles: Aggressive → Progressive → Secured → Conservative.
4 Investment Styles: Accumulation → Consolidation → Spending → Gifting and Charity.
Young age = Aggressive risk profile = Accumulation investment style.
Near retirement = Conservative risk profile = Gifting and Charity investment style.
Inflation = Rise in prices = EROSION of money value = LESS purchasing power (NOT more).
Insurance Purchase is NOT a strategy to maximize discretionary income.
Housing Loans do NOT form part of Insurance Planning.
Contingency Products address UNCERTAINTIES — not cash needs or wealth creation.
